questions.stem: Case O: A 50 kg patient receives a ketamine infusion at 0.15 mg/kg/hr. What is the hourly infusion rate?
questions.explanation: 0.15 mg/kg/hr × 50 kg = 7.5 mg/hr.

questions.stem: Case P: A patient receives a block with 25 mL 0.5% ropivacaine. What is the dose?
Case P: The surgeon adds 20 mL 0.25% ropivacaine. What is the added dose?
A patient scheduled for inguinal hernia repair asks why long-term pain is discussed for a relatively routine operation. Which response is MOST accurate?
options: Inguinal herniorrhaphy is among procedures associated with chronic postsurgical pain
Chronic postsurgical pain occurs only after amputations
Hernia repair has no recognized chronic-pain risk
Chronic pain is limited to oncologic surgery
questions.explanation: Inguinal herniorrhaphy is among procedures associated with chronic postsurgical pain.

questions.stem: For a procedure associated with chronic postsurgical pain, which preventive strategy is MOST consistent with limiting central sensitization?
options: Provide analgesia with sufficient depth and field coverage that extends into the postoperative period
Avoid perioperative analgesia to prevent tolerance
Wait until emergence to begin opioid therapy
Avoid regional techniques because they mask early chronic pain
questions.explanation: Preventive analgesia aims to block central sensitization.

questions.stem: An older adult with mild cognitive impairment becomes intermittently confused after repeated opioid doses. Which age-related concern should MOST influence further treatment?
options: Greater vulnerability to oversedation and delirium requires cautious titration and reassessment
Older age reliably produces opioid tolerance
Higher pain tolerance requires larger routine opioid doses
Faster drug metabolism shortens every opioid effect
questions.explanation: Elderly patients have altered drug metabolism and cognitive vulnerability.

questions.stem: Case R: A 68-year-old has mild cognitive impairment and is receiving opioids. What approach is BEST?
options: Lower doses, careful titration, and multimodal adjuncts
Standard adult doses, since pain threshold rises with age
questions.explanation: Titrate carefully in geriatric patients.

questions.stem: A patient taking an SSRI becomes agitated and tachycardic after tramadol. Which pharmacologic property makes this combination concerning?
options: Tramadol has serotonergic/norepinephrine reuptake effects in addition to opioid activity
Tramadol is a pure mu agonist with no monoamine effect
Tramadol directly antagonizes SSRIs and precipitates opioid withdrawal
Tramadol is a local anesthetic that causes systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Tramadol has SNRI activity and interactions.

questions.stem: Case S: The patient on an SSRI developed agitation and tachycardia after tramadol. What lesson applies to tramadol?
options: It is safe with all antidepressants
It is a pure mu agonist with no monoamine activity
questions.explanation: Tramadol has SNRI activity and CYP2D6 dependence, creating many interactions.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient arrives for surgery with a PCA already in use. Before adding anesthetic opioids, which information is MOST important?
options: Recent delivered doses and timing, along with the current PCA regimen
Only the programmed settings, regardless of doses actually received
questions.explanation: Know last dose/time of analgesics that affect your plan.

questions.stem: Case T: A patient with chronic pain arrives on a PCA. What is the risk of ignoring prior PCA dosing?
options: Oversedation or withdrawal due to mismatched dosing
No change in outcomes, since the OR plan overrides PCA
questions.explanation: Prior dosing affects safety and effectiveness of your plan.

questions.stem: After laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a patient has shoulder-tip pain without shoulder injury. Which mechanism BEST explains the symptom?
options: Referred visceral pain from diaphragmatic/peritoneal irritation
Superficial somatic pain from shoulder skin
Peripheral neuropathy from surgical transection at the shoulder
Deep somatic pain from bone injury
questions.explanation: Visceral pain can be referred to the shoulder.

questions.stem: Case U: A patient undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy and has referred shoulder pain. Which intervention may help?
options: Stop all analgesics until the pain localizes
questions.explanation: Nonpharmacologic interventions and multimodal analgesia help.

questions.stem: Soon after neuraxial fentanyl, a patient develops clinically significant hypoventilation. Which response has priority?
options: Support ventilation and titrate naloxone if opioid reversal is required
Wait because only delayed respiratory depression is clinically important
Administer more fentanyl to prevent withdrawal
Give flumazenil as the opioid antagonist
questions.explanation: Early respiratory depression from fentanyl needs airway support and possible naloxone.

questions.stem: Case V: A patient receives neuraxial fentanyl and develops early respiratory depression. Why is fentanyl's effect early?
questions.explanation: Lipophilic opioids act quickly.

questions.stem: Case W: A patient has pain and hypertension after a tourniquet. What should you do first?
options: Assess for tourniquet pain and treat appropriately
Increase fluids, since hypertension reflects hypovolemia
Treat as expected hypertension and continue
questions.explanation: Assess pain source; tourniquet pain is common.

questions.stem: A patient with tourniquet discomfort becomes hypertensive but is also newly hypoxemic. Which problem takes priority before escalating analgesia?
options: Give opioid first because hypertension proves pain is primary
Give NSAID first because it cannot affect ventilation
Treat the blood pressure without addressing oxygenation
questions.explanation: Hypoxemia is a pain differential to treat first.

questions.stem: Case X: A patient on methadone arrives for surgery. What is a key consideration?
questions.explanation: Methadone response varies with CYP2D6, OPRM1, and ABCB1.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on methadone presents for a painful operation. Which strategy BEST separates maintenance therapy from the additional surgical analgesic requirement?
options: Continue baseline methadone and add individualized multimodal perioperative analgesia
Stop all opioids until postoperative pain is measurable
Use acetaminophen alone because maintenance methadone covers surgical pain
questions.explanation: Continue baseline opioid and add multimodal analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient reports a 'morphine allergy' consisting only of prior generalized itching without swelling, bronchospasm, or hypotension. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Clarify and document the reaction as a likely opioid adverse effect rather than automatically labeling anaphylaxis
Treat the historical event as active anaphylaxis
Give prophylactic epinephrine before any opioid
questions.explanation: Itching is an adverse effect, not true allergy.

questions.stem: Case Y: A patient reports "morphine allergy" with itching only. If the patient reports facial swelling and vomiting, what does this suggest?
options: A normal opioid effect needing observation
questions.explanation: Erythema and facial swelling suggest true allergy.

questions.stem: A PACU patient reports pain 8/10 but repeatedly falls asleep and has a respiratory rate of 8/min after opioid therapy. Which action BEST balances the pain report with immediate safety?
options: Reassess arousal and ventilation and withhold further opioid until respiratory safety is established
Give a large opioid bolus because self-reported pain always overrides sedation
Administer naloxone automatically without assessing ventilation
Ignore the pain score because sleeping proves the patient is comfortable
questions.explanation: Reassess arousal and respiratory status before giving more.

questions.stem: Case Z: A patient in PACU has pain and a pain score of 8, but is sleeping and RR 8. What does this scenario illustrate?
options: Pain scores are accurate even when asleep
questions.explanation: Continuous reassessment prevents over-administration.

questions.stem: A severely anxious PACU patient hyperventilates and reports 10/10 pain despite substantial opioid already producing adequate analgesic exposure. Which next step BEST avoids compounding opioid toxicity?
options: Address anxiety with reassurance and an appropriate nonopioid/anxiolytic strategy while reassessing pain
Continue escalating opioid until the patient sleeps
Withhold all treatment because anxiety invalidates the pain report
Remove monitoring to reduce environmental stimulation
questions.explanation: Anxiety amplifies pain, and treating it is a non-opioid intervention.

questions.stem: A patient's pain is uncontrolled and she is at high risk for inadequate control. What guideline applies?
questions.explanation: Guideline 7 supports pain specialist consultation.

questions.stem: An epidural that had provided good analgesia stops functioning and breakthrough pain develops. Which next step BEST avoids compounding toxicity from a rescue modality?
options: Reassess the epidural and patient, then add or change therapy with attention to overlapping effects
Increase every epidural medication without checking the catheter or block
Stop all analgesia to determine the true pain score
Give naloxone before troubleshooting the epidural
questions.explanation: Adding a second modality requires care.

questions.stem: A patient becomes apneic after receiving both opioid and benzodiazepine. Which intervention takes priority before deciding which reversal drug to use?
questions.explanation: Airway support comes first; reversal may follow.

questions.stem: During an IV lidocaine infusion, a patient reports new circumoral numbness and metallic taste. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Suspect early local-anesthetic systemic toxicity, stop the infusion, and assess immediately
Continue because these are expected analgesic endpoints
Treat empirically for hypocalcemia without changing lidocaine
questions.explanation: Perioral numbness suggests LAST; stop the infusion and assess.

questions.stem: A peripheral nerve block is proposed in a room without immediate airway/resuscitation equipment or lipid emulsion. Which safety concern should determine whether to proceed?
options: A serious block complication could occur before rescue resources arrive
Remote placement reduces complications because there are fewer interruptions
Emergency equipment is unnecessary for ultrasound-guided blocks
Lowering the local-anesthetic dose eliminates the need for rescue capability
questions.explanation: Regional anesthesia requires emergency equipment.

questions.stem: A patient receives low-dose ketamine and reports vivid dreams. What should you consider?
questions.explanation: Ketamine can cause dissociative effects.

questions.stem: During a magnesium analgesic infusion, a patient shows greater-than-expected weakness after a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Which interaction should be suspected?
options: Acute opioid tolerance caused by magnesium
questions.explanation: Magnesium can enhance neuromuscular blockade and weakness.

questions.stem: A patient wearing a transdermal fentanyl patch is placed under an active warming device during a long operation. Which pharmacokinetic concern is MOST important?
options: Heat can increase transdermal fentanyl absorption and opioid exposure
questions.explanation: Warming can increase transdermal absorption, raising opioid levels.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient with severe anxiety and PTSD is scheduled for major surgery. Why should these comorbidities be addressed in the perioperative pain plan?
options: Psychological comorbidity can amplify pain experience and complicate analgesic management
Psychiatric symptoms should be deferred until surgical pain resolves
Opioids alone reliably treat both chronic pain and PTSD
Regional techniques are contraindicated when anxiety is present
questions.explanation: Managing anxiety, PTSD, and depression is part of effective pain care in chronic pain patients.

questions.stem: After spine surgery, a patient describes burning pain radiating down the leg with electric shocks and allodynia. Which mechanism should be specifically targeted in addition to routine incisional analgesia?
questions.explanation: Burning and radiating pain suggests neuropathic features.

questions.stem: A patient's pain assessment shows it worsens with coughing. What does this identify?
questions.explanation: Exacerbating factors make pain start or worsen.

questions.stem: A patient says ice helps her pain. What does this identify?
questions.explanation: Relieving factors make pain better.

questions.stem: A patient says pain interferes with walking. Which assessment feature is this?
options: Interference with activities of daily living
Radiation of the pain into the leg or buttock
questions.explanation: Pain assessment includes interference with ADLs.

questions.stem: After hernia repair, a patient is diaphoretic and nauseated but reports pain 2/10. Which interpretation BEST avoids unnecessary opioid administration?
options: Autonomic and gastrointestinal signs are nonspecific and may have causes other than pain
Sweating and nausea prove severe pain despite the patient's report
Patient self-report should be ignored when autonomic signs are present
Nausea is the most specific physiologic measure of postoperative pain
questions.explanation: Nausea and sweating may reflect other causes, so the patient's report is preferred.

questions.stem: A unit routinely substitutes clinicians' visual estimates for patient-reported pain scores. Which error is MOST likely?
options: Systematic observer bias related to experience and assumptions
More accurate assessment than patient self-report
Elimination of cultural influences on pain assessment
questions.explanation: Staff estimates are biased by experience, so patient self-report is preferred.

questions.stem: A patient's pain management plan is agreed on by patient, surgeon, and anesthesia. Which note principle is this?
options: Plan developed in the PACU after emergence
questions.explanation: The plan should be agreed on by patient, surgeon, and anesthesia.

questions.stem: A thoracic epidural will require a higher-acuity postoperative location and specialized follow-up. When should these resources be secured?
options: Before surgery as part of the analgesic plan
After PACU arrival if the epidural still works
Only after the first breakthrough-pain episode
questions.explanation: Extended plans need coordination before entering the OR.

questions.stem: A patient receives opioids and has constipation. Which adverse effect category is this?
questions.explanation: Constipation is a listed adverse effect.

questions.stem: A patient has anaphylaxis after an analgesic. Which category is this?
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a listed adverse effect.

questions.stem: A patient receives opioids and has urinary retention. What should be done?
options: Continue, since retention is expected and self-limited
questions.explanation: Urinary retention is a listed adverse effect; manage appropriately.

questions.stem: After colectomy, morphine monotherapy controls pain poorly and causes severe nausea and constipation. Which change BEST improves the therapeutic balance?
options: Add nonopioid and/or regional multimodal strategies to reduce opioid requirement
Increase morphine and add a basal PCA infusion
Stop antiemetics so nausea can guide opioid titration
Avoid all nonopioid agents to prevent drug interactions
questions.explanation: Multimodal combinations lower opioid doses and their side effects.

questions.stem: A patient's pain is controlled with acetaminophen and NSAIDs. What does this demonstrate?
options: Improved analgesia and reduced opioid consumption
Higher respiratory depression risk from the combination
questions.explanation: Combining acetaminophen with NSAIDs improves analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient with significant renal impairment is receiving ketorolac as part of a multimodal regimen. Which adjustment is MOST appropriate?
options: Reconsider the NSAID and use renal-appropriate multimodal alternatives
Increase ketorolac because renal impairment reduces its effect
Continue the standard regimen without reassessment
Add morphine specifically to protect renal function
questions.explanation: NSAIDs may be limited in renal impairment; choose alternatives.

questions.stem: A 75-kg patient has received no other local anesthetic. The surgeon requests 30 mL of 1% plain lidocaine. Using a maximum of about 4.5 mg/kg, which assessment is correct?
options: 300 mg is below the calculated ~337.5 mg limit, but cumulative dosing must still be tracked
300 mg exceeds a calculated 225 mg limit
questions.explanation: 1% = 10 mg/mL × 30 = 300 mg; 4.5 × 75 ≈ 337 mg. It fits only if no other local anesthetic has been given.

questions.stem: A patient receives 20 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine for an interscalene block, then the surgeon requests another 20 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine for infiltration. What cumulative dose must be evaluated against the patient's safe limit?
questions.explanation: 0.5% = 5 mg/mL; 40 mL × 5 = 200 mg total, which must be checked against the weight-based max.

questions.stem: A 60 kg woman is on a plan with ketamine 0.2 mg/kg then 0.15 mg/kg/hr and magnesium 50 mg/kg then 8 mg/kg/hr. Which set is correct?
options: Ketamine 12 mg then 9 mg/hr; Mg 3 g then 480 mg/hr
Ketamine 6 mg then 4.5 mg/hr; Mg 1.5 g then 240 mg/hr
Ketamine 24 mg then 18 mg/hr; Mg 6 g then 960 mg/hr
Ketamine 12 mg then 90 mg/hr; Mg 300 mg then 48 mg/hr

questions.stem: A PACU patient becomes somnolent with RR 6/min and SpO2 90% after hydromorphone and midazolam. Which sequence BEST prioritizes immediate safety while attempting to preserve analgesia?
options: Support ventilation first, consider flumazenil for the benzodiazepine, then titrate naloxone if opioid reversal remains necessary
Give a large naloxone dose before supporting ventilation
Give dexmedetomidine before either reversal drug
questions.explanation: Airway support comes first; reversing the benzodiazepine before naloxone may avoid abrupt pain.

questions.stem: During emergence after laparotomy, an intubated patient is coughing, hypertensive, has dilated pupils, and breathes 26/min with adequate neuromuscular recovery. Which response BEST balances analgesia with extubation safety?
options: Carefully titrate opioid while reassessing ventilation and extubation readiness rather than treating blood pressure alone
Give a large opioid bolus solely to normalize blood pressure
Deepen volatile anesthesia and extubate regardless of readiness
questions.explanation: Titrate to RR and pupils; avoid treating vital signs alone with large opioid doses.

questions.stem: A femoral nerve catheter provides excellent resting analgesia, but knee pain prevents participation in physical therapy. Which conclusion BEST guides adjustment of the plan?
options: Analgesic success should include functional pain with movement, not resting pain alone
The block is adequate because resting pain is controlled
Movement-related pain should not influence postoperative analgesia
The catheter should be removed because any movement pain proves block toxicity
questions.explanation: Consider pain with movement and breathing.

questions.stem: A patient reports pain 9/10 while HR is 72/min and BP is 118/70 mm Hg. Which principle should govern the assessment?
options: Normal vital signs do not exclude severe pain; the patient's report remains central
Normal vital signs prove the pain is exaggerated
Analgesia should wait until sympathetic signs develop
Blood pressure is more reliable than self-report
questions.explanation: The best measure is the patient's perception.

questions.stem: Which patient combines both a procedure strongly associated with chronic postsurgical pain and a modifiable perioperative risk factor?
options: A thoracotomy patient with severe poorly controlled acute postoperative pain
A laparoscopic appendectomy patient with effective analgesia
A cataract patient with minimal discomfort
A carpal-tunnel patient with well-controlled pain
questions.explanation: Thoracotomy and poorly controlled acute pain are both strong risk factors for chronic postsurgical pain.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on buprenorphine has severe postoperative pain despite nonopioid adjuncts. Which strategy BEST avoids precipitating withdrawal while treating the new pain burden?
options: Continue buprenorphine and add appropriate full-mu agonist and multimodal therapy as needed
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine may continue with full agonist supplementation.

questions.stem: A physically opioid-dependent patient with only mild sedation receives a large naloxone dose and becomes acutely agitated, hypertensive, and tachycardic. Which error MOST directly caused the deterioration?
options: Excessive antagonist dosing precipitated withdrawal; naloxone should be titrated to the minimum effect needed
questions.explanation: Naloxone can precipitate withdrawal in dependent patients.

questions.stem: A short procedure is induced with a large fentanyl bolus, and the patient remains slow to emerge after the surgery ends quickly. Which planning principle was missed?
options: Match opioid onset, peak, and duration to the intensity and length of surgical stimulation
Use additional opioid at emergence to accelerate redistribution
Prefer long-acting opioids for all short procedures
questions.explanation: Timing and duration must match the procedure.

questions.stem: Ketorolac is given early during a vascular procedure before bleeding risk and surgical hemostasis are clarified. Which planning principle was missed?
options: Coordinate NSAID timing with the surgeon and bleeding context, often near the end of the case
NSAIDs should always be given at induction
NSAID timing is unrelated to surgical bleeding considerations
NSAIDs should replace all opioid therapy
questions.explanation: The lecture says no NSAIDs until the end and discuss with the surgeon.

questions.stem: The surgeon begins closing after a laparoscopic hernia repair and has not injected local anesthetic. What should you do?
options: Remind the surgeon to infiltrate before emergence
Give extra IV opioid at emergence
questions.explanation: Local infiltration before emergence provides early analgesia and spares opioids.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving dexmedetomidine and hydromorphone and becomes excessively sedated. Which reversal is possible?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine cannot be reversed; opioids can be reversed with naloxone.

questions.stem: Which drug class is recommended for neuropathic components after amputation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Neuropathic pain benefits from α2–δ ligands, NMDA antagonists, and α2 agonists.

questions.stem: A PCA patient has reached the programmed 1-hour hydromorphone limit yet continues to report severe pain. Which action BEST distinguishes undertreatment from unsafe escalation?
options: Reassess pain mechanism, sedation, ventilation, PCA use, and the broader analgesic plan before changing settings
Add a large basal infusion without reassessment
Stop the PCA and administer naloxone
questions.explanation: The PCA should be adjusted based on assessment and safety.

questions.stem: A patient receives opioids and becomes hypotensive with a HR of 50. What should be checked first?
options: Pain score and last opioid dose
questions.explanation: Assess rhythm and BP before treating bradycardia.

questions.stem: A patient with significant renal impairment requires postoperative analgesia. Which strategy BEST minimizes avoidable renal and metabolite-related risk?
options: Acetaminophen plus appropriate regional/nonopioid techniques, with individualized opioid selection if needed
Morphine PCA with a routine basal infusion
questions.explanation: Avoid NSAIDs and renally cleared opioids; use acetaminophen and regional options.

questions.stem: During an IV lidocaine infusion, a patient develops tinnitus and circumoral paresthesia. Which action has priority?
options: Stop lidocaine and evaluate immediately for local-anesthetic systemic toxicity
Increase the infusion because symptoms indicate inadequate effect
Continue unchanged because these are desired analgesic effects
questions.explanation: Tinnitus is an early LAST sign; stop the infusion.

questions.stem: A patient receives dexamethasone for PONV and analgesia. What is a planning consideration?
options: Plan timing based on onset and effects
Avoid in all diabetics without discussion
questions.explanation: The lecture asks when to dose dexamethasone.

questions.stem: A patient with a dense peripheral nerve block is being discharged and fears severe pain when sensation returns overnight. Which instruction BEST prevents a gap in analgesia?
options: Begin the planned oral multimodal regimen before the block fully resolves
Wait until severe pain returns before taking medication
Assume the block will last at least 72 hours
Delay all medication until normal sensation is completely restored
questions.explanation: Educate patients to start analgesics before block resolution.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic pain uses gabapentin daily. Should it be continued?
options: Consider continuing as part of the multimodal plan
Stop it the week before surgery
Double it the morning of surgery
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes continuing vs holding routine meds and multimodal use.

questions.stem: A highly opioid-tolerant patient is rotated to methadone after poor response to escalating doses of another opioid. Which property may make methadone useful beyond simple mu agonism?
options: NMDA-receptor antagonism may help address tolerance/hyperalgesic mechanisms
It is a mixed mu antagonist-kappa agonist
It depends primarily on renal activation
questions.explanation: Methadone is a common rotation choice and also antagonizes NMDA receptors.

questions.stem: A thoracic epidural provides excellent analgesia but the patient becomes hypotensive. Which mechanism should be assessed along with intravascular volume?
questions.explanation: Epidural local anesthetics can cause hypotension via sympathectomy.

questions.stem: A chronic-opioid patient is scheduled for major surgery. Which preoperative step is MOST important before designing supplemental intraoperative and postoperative opioid doses?
options: Determine the baseline daily opioid requirement/equivalent and build a multimodal plan around it
Stop opioids for 48 hours to reduce tolerance
Assume regional anesthesia eliminates the baseline requirement
Give naltrexone to rapidly reverse tolerance
questions.explanation: Tolerant patients need baseline calculation and multimodal plans.

questions.stem: A continuous peripheral nerve catheter becomes disconnected, and a previously comfortable patient develops abrupt severe pain. Which interpretation BEST guides treatment?
options: Loss of continuous regional analgesia caused return or rebound of pain; restore/troubleshoot the block while providing bridge analgesia
The abrupt pain is the expected course and needs no intervention
Stopping local anesthetic caused opioid toxicity
The event indicates local-anesthetic systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Interrupting CPNB causes pain return.

questions.stem: A young woman with high PONV risk undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Which analgesic strategy BEST addresses both pain and a major modifiable PONV contributor?
options: Use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia with appropriate antiemetic prophylaxis
Use high-dose systemic opioid with a basal PCA
Use morphine PCA as the primary strategy
questions.explanation: Multimodal regimens reduce opioid-related PONV.

questions.stem: A patient has visceral pain after bowel surgery. Which description fits?
options: Sharp, well localized, and throbbing at the incision
questions.explanation: Visceral pain from organs is often poorly localized or referred.

questions.stem: A patient has shooting pain along the leg after spine surgery. What type is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Shooting pain along a nerve distribution suggests peripheral neuropathic pain.

questions.stem: A long-term opioid user reports progressively worse diffuse pain as opioid doses are repeatedly increased. Which possibility should prompt a change in strategy rather than automatic dose escalation?
options: Expected improvement from higher opioid exposure
A need for mixed agonist-antagonists in every patient
questions.explanation: Increasing doses with worsening pain suggest tolerance or hyperalgesia.

questions.stem: A patient's pain plan includes both short- and long-acting opioids for PACU. Why?
options: To reduce PACU costs and nursing time per patient
To avoid multimodal agents and simplify PACU orders
To avoid all opioid side effects
questions.explanation: PACU orders generally need both.

questions.stem: An epidural infusion contains both local anesthetic and opioid. Compared with a local-anesthetic-only technique, which postoperative safety issue requires particular attention?
options: Respiratory depression from neuraxial opioid exposure
No additional monitoring issue once PACU discharge criteria are met
Loss of all motor function regardless of concentration
questions.explanation: Neuraxial opioids change postoperative monitoring requirements.

questions.stem: A family asks why aggressive but safe postoperative pain control matters beyond comfort. Which answer BEST connects analgesia to recovery?
options: Uncontrolled pain can impair pulmonary, cardiovascular, functional, and overall recovery
Pain control changes comfort but not physiologic outcomes
Analgesia primarily shortens the operation itself
Treating pain generally delays mobilization and recovery
questions.explanation: Poorly managed acute pain has multiple adverse physiologic consequences.
